name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Sunday 12 January 1992 (English cryptic)

clue.text: Composer is in a bit of despair always

indicators.note: a bit of a word here is just its opening letter, the smallest piece you can take
one word sitting in another means it is placed inside that word's letters

blocks.note: the first letter of despair
always means for ever
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy composer, forever mired in despair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composer' looks like a musician, but here it is anyone who composes, that is devises, something.
explanation.definitionFit: A deviser is someone who puts something together or invents it, which is what a composer literally does.

clue.text: Sweet potatoes I'd served up, causing trepidation

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters read from the bottom upwards, so the order turns round

blocks.note: yams are sweet potatoes in American usage
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A cook frets about the sweet potatoes being dished up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served up' sounds like dishing out food, but in a down clue it turns the letters upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismay is a sinking feeling of alarm and distress, close to trepidation.

clue.text: Conceit — one finds it in Navy, oddly enough

indicators.note: oddly means in a strange way, so these letters come out in a strange order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram material
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A remark that pride is surprisingly common among naval officers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a hidden-word signal, but the letters are not consecutive in the clue; 'it' and 'Navy' are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: Conceit is an excessive pride in oneself, which is what vanity means.

clue.text: Most bad-tempered, knocked over wine and pastries in the street

indicators.note: a glass knocked over ends upside down, and in a down entry that turns the word's order
in places the preceding pieces inside the following word

blocks.note: port is a fortified wine
pies are pastries
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: The grumpiest customer, who knocked over the wine and pies in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: To strop is British slang for a sulk or tantrum, so the stroppiest person is the most bad-tempered.
explanation.definitionFit: Stroppy is British informal for bad-tempered and argumentative; this is its superlative.

clue.text: Battalion's leader, captured in attack, is furious

indicators.note: a word's leader is the letter at its front, so only that one is taken
something captured in another thing is held inside it

blocks.note: the first letter of Battalion
a raid is a sudden attack

explanation.surface: The battalion commander, taken prisoner during an attack, is livid.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabid literally describes an animal with rabies; figuratively it means wildly and violently angry.

clue.text: Go the wrong way, pinching pennies, getting caught

definitions.note: the answer is a past participle while the definition is an -ing form; both describe being caught

indicators.note: going the wrong way means running backwards, so the word is read from its end
to pinch something is to grip it, so one word holds another inside it

blocks.note: to go is to depart
P is the abbreviation for pence or pennies

explanation.surface: A miser goes the wrong way about saving pennies and gets caught out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' looks like part of the phrase 'go the wrong way', but it is the word to turn round: DEPART backwards is TRAPED, which takes in P to make TRAPPED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone trapped has been caught, as an animal is in a snare.

clue.text: See the difference between Archer and a character on stage?

blocks.note: William Tell is the legendary Swiss archer
taken as written
an actor's part is the character played

explanation.surface: A puzzle asking how a real archer differs from an actor playing one.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'the difference between' is part of the definition, not a subtraction. The scanned page shows 'Sec', a misread of 'See'.
explanation.definitionFit: To tell two things apart is to distinguish them, seeing what makes them different.

clue.text: Foreign money raised for seed-covering

indicators.note: raised means lifted upward, and in a down entry that reads the word from bottom to top

blocks.note: the lira was the currency of Italy

explanation.surface: Foreign cash being raised to pay for seed.
explanation.walkthrough: The lira was Italy's currency until the euro arrived in 2002.
explanation.definitionFit: An aril is a fleshy outer coat around some seeds, such as the red cup on a yew berry.

clue.text: Publicity agent given leaflet to lengthen

blocks.note: a PRO is a public relations officer
a tract is a short pamphlet, often religious or political

explanation.surface: A press agent handed a pamphlet to pad out.
explanation.definitionFit: To protract something is to draw it out in time, which is to lengthen it.

clue.text: Thirsty, drinking a lime excitedly, in imagination

indicators.note: something done excitedly is done in a jumble, so these letters are mixed up
to drink something is to take it inside, so one word holds the other

blocks.note: dry means thirsty
a lime as anagram material

explanation.surface: A thirsty person gulping a lime drink, lost in a daydream.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something dreamily is doing it as if in a dream, with the mind in a world of fancy.

clue.text: Detecting apparatus like this operated in retreat

indicators.note: an army in retreat goes back the way it came, so this word is read backwards

blocks.note: 'like this' means 'so', as in 'do it so'
to operate a business is to run it

explanation.surface: Detection equipment that works like this while the army falls back.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second piece turns round; the first stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonar detects objects underwater by sending out sound pulses and timing their echoes.

clue.text: A junior officer, I'm gripped by a tedious fellow in Maryland

definitions.note: the definition is a place description, a city in Maryland, standing for the city's name

indicators.note: something gripped by another thing is held inside it, so the earlier pieces go inside the later one

blocks.note: taken as written
LT is the abbreviation for lieutenant, a junior officer
taken as written, apostrophe dropped
a bore is a tedious person

explanation.surface: A junior officer complains of being stuck with a boring man while posted in Maryland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Maryland' reads as where the scene happens, but it is the definition: a city in that state.
explanation.definitionFit: Baltimore is the largest city in the US state of Maryland.

clue.text: Possibly Australian worker I criticise severely about poem

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for criticising goes around the poem

blocks.note: the worker ant is the crossword's standard worker
taken as written
to pan a show is to slate it
an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: An Australian labourer admits to savaging a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' marks Australian as one example: the antipodes are the lands on the opposite side of the globe from Britain, chiefly Australia and New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipodean describes things from Australia or New Zealand, so an Australian is one possible case.

clue.text: Forbidding king to enter returning fighter plane

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the plane's name is read from its end
to enter something is to go inside it, so the king sits within the other word

blocks.note: the MiG is a Russian fighter jet
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A stern refusal to let the king board a fighter jet on its way back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forbidding' looks like a verb of refusal, but it is the adjective meaning stern and threatening.
explanation.definitionFit: A forbidding look is a stern, unwelcoming one, which is a grim look.

clue.text: Reinforce English, in strait at that time

blocks.note: STR is the abbreviation for strait on maps
ENG is the abbreviation for English
then means at that time

explanation.surface: The English reinforce their position in a narrow sea passage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal, but ENG follows STR; the setter uses it loosely to join the two abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: To strengthen something is to make it stronger, which is what reinforcing it does.

clue.text: Critical map, badly crumpled, is unusable

indicators.note: a map badly crumpled is creased out of shape, so these letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram material
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: An important map has been so badly crumpled that nobody can use it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something impractical cannot work in real use, so it is in effect unusable.

clue.text: Was mother at tea-party for French editor abroad?

blocks.note: pour is French for 'for'
ED is the abbreviation for editor
out means away from home, abroad

explanation.surface: Did a French editor posted overseas play mother at a tea party?
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, the one who pours the tea is said to 'be mother'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being mother at a tea party means serving the tea, so whoever did it poured out.

clue.text: Cisco frolicking with orc gets quite a blow

indicators.note: frolicking means romping about playfully, so the letters jump out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram material
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: The Cisco Kid, playing about with a monster, gets a heavy punch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' looks like a punch, but it is a wind. The scanned page shows 'ore', a misread of 'orc'.
explanation.definitionFit: The scirocco is a hot, strong wind blowing from North Africa across the Mediterranean, so quite a blow.

clue.text: Slab, dull, is used as stand for dishes

blocks.note: a table can mean a flat slab, as of stone
mat, also spelt matt, means having a dull surface

explanation.surface: A dull slab of stone pressed into service to hold the dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: A table mat is placed under plates or hot dishes to protect the table's surface.

clue.text: Commander requires almost everyone to sink the vessel

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: CO is commanding officer
everyone means all
to scuttle a ship is to sink it deliberately

explanation.surface: A naval commander demands that nearly the whole crew help sink the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The vessel' looks like the ship being sunk, but the word for sinking is the wordplay and the vessel is the definition: a scuttle is also a bucket.
explanation.definitionFit: A coal scuttle is a metal container for carrying coal to the fire, so it is a household vessel.

clue.text: Rich silk fabric, it covers a small child

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece that covers another sits above it, so it comes first

blocks.note: 'it' is old slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
a mite is a tiny child

explanation.surface: A luxurious silk wrapped around a little one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' meaning sex appeal comes from the 1920s 'It girl'; its abbreviation is SA.
explanation.definitionFit: Samite is a heavy silk fabric, often woven with gold thread, worn in the Middle Ages.

clue.text: The man curses being capless in the moors

indicators.note: without a cap means the top is gone, and the top of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the man is he
oaths are curses or swear words

explanation.surface: A hatless man swearing as he crosses the moors.
explanation.definitionFit: A heath is open, uncultivated land covered with heather and scrub, much like a moor.

clue.text: A rattling sound in a camera lens

indicators.note: in tells you the letters sit inside the following words, running across the space

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Something rattling about inside a camera lens.
explanation.definitionFit: A rale is a medical term for a rattling sound heard in the lungs through a stethoscope.

clue.text: Degenerating, making bad error, gated

indicators.note: something gone bad has been spoiled, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram material
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A gated community declining, its errors piling up.
explanation.walkthrough: The scanned page shows 'baa', a misread of 'bad'.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrograde can mean going backwards or declining into a worse state, which is degenerating.

clue.text: Red setter

blocks.note: first meaning: a Latin word for red or red-haired, used as a name
second meaning: the pen name of a famous crossword compiler

explanation.walkthrough: 'Red setter' suggests the dog breed; instead it is two senses of one name. Roger Squires set crosswords as Rufus for decades.
explanation.definitionFit: Rufus is Latin for red-haired, and it was the pseudonym of the prolific crossword compiler Roger Squires.

clue.text: An up-and-down girl

indicators.note: reading the same upward and downward in a down entry means the name mirrors itself

blocks.note: surface reading: a moody young woman, cheerful one day and low the next
setter's reading: the name reads the same from top to bottom as from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A girl whose moods swing up and down.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests mood swings; the instruction is to find a girl's name that is a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna is a common female first name, so it serves for girl.

clue.text: Proving successful? Closing down

blocks.note: first meaning: a plan that works is said to do this
second meaning: what a show does when its run ends

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes it sound like a business doing well before it shuts; the two halves are separate senses of one phrase, the second from the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme coming off has worked out, and a play coming off is ending its run and closing.

clue.text: Ambassador is initially tried for theft

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: HE is His Excellency, the formal title of an ambassador
taken as written
the first letter of tried

explanation.surface: A diplomat put on trial for stealing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an ambassador in court; the letters come from his title, His Excellency.
explanation.definitionFit: A heist is a robbery, especially a daring one, so it is a theft.

clue.text: Survive, not dismissed until end of team's innings

definitions.text: not dismissed until end of team's innings

blocks.note: first meaning: live or last longer than something

blocks.clueFragment: not dismissed until end of team's innings
blocks.note: second meaning, read as two words: a batter who is dismissed last of the side

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batter is 'out' when dismissed; one who stays in until the innings ends is the last one out, read here as OUT LAST.
explanation.definitionFit: To outlast is to keep going longer than something else, which is to survive it.

clue.text: Summer's beginning, if not lacking in brightness overhead

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of Summer
unless means if not

explanation.surface: A summer that starts out without much sunshine.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunless sky is grey overhead, with no sun to give it brightness.
